paras: The Chicago Heights race-riot scare was a period of reported conflict between Italian and Black residents of Chicago Heights, Illinois, in early August 1920, during which deputy sheriffs patrolled the town and a National Guard company was mobilized. Wire services reported rioting and a Black exodus, but the police chief, the mayor and the Black press called the reports exaggerated or false. The episode became chiefly a dispute over the press, with the Chicago Whip charging that a Hearst daily had invented it.

According to a Universal Service dispatch, Italians in the town objected to Black people moving into white districts and replacing striking factory workers. The Associated Negro Press (ANP) put the number of Black steel mill workers at about three thousand, amid a strike among the Italians. Chief of Police Thomas Stone said minor street fights had occurred for two years, fed by dissatisfaction among "the foreign elements" with Black residents in the Italian and Hungarian districts. Wire reports also cited a hearsay report that two Black men had attacked an Italian girl days earlier.

On August 6 the United Press reported that twenty-five deputies had been rushed to the town over reported race riots, though no trouble had yet occurred. It said 500 white and 3,500 Black residents had left in three days after Italians threatened to "get even" for an Italian's murder by a Hungarian, and that Italians gathered at a Hungarian's home were reported to be after a Black man. A Universal Service dispatch that night gave fifteen deputies, an armed guard company ready to leave Chicago, Black residents leaving "in droves" and disturbances in the factory district, but no fatalities.

On August 7 the Lake County Times of nearby Hammond, Indiana, reported Company L waiting at the local armory and quoted Mayor E. G. Klinger that trouble makers "in both parties" were leaving. The ANP later described the only fight as one between a Black family and "a few Italians" who came to their house looking for a Hungarian accused of killing an Italian, who had rented the house to the family.

Stone called the affair mostly rumor, and police blamed radical agitators. The guard company was not sent onto the streets, and by August 12 feeling was reported to have quieted. No report of arrests over the disturbances appears in the coverage.

Late on August 11 an Italian man known as Frank was found dying of gunshot wounds near Chicago Heights and, according to the Lake County Times, whispered that he had been shot by "a negro named Taylor." Police thought the killing might be connected with the trouble.

A United Press item headed "Race Riot Reported" ran on August 6, and the Universal Service dispatch ran in the Richmond Times-Dispatch and the Washington Herald on August 7. The Richmond headline read "Italians Drive Negroes in Droves From Chicago Heights Following Attempted Assault." An Associated Press story quoting Stone followed under heads such as "Chicago Heights Riots Minimized" and "No Rioting in Chicago Heights," yet weeklies in North Dakota and Nevada repeated the rioting and alleged attack on August 12 and 14.

The Black press treated the story as a fabrication. On August 14 the Chicago Whip's front page, headed "Daily Paper Invents Story," charged that W. R. Hearst's Herald-Examiner had manufactured the riot and said its investigators found the town peaceful. The Whip quoted Stone blaming "the commercialized press" for inspiring mob violence, Dr. E. H. Chandler, a Black chemist, denying any exodus, and Klinger calling the report a fake by political enemies; a column lashed white reporters who blamed Black residents for the trouble. An ANP item in the Cleveland Advocate and Tulsa Star called the riot "without foundation," and the Baltimore Afro-American reported no riots.

The Universal Service reported rioting, while Stone, Klinger, Chandler and the ANP, closer to the scene, denied it. Two printings of the ANP item differ on Deputy Sheriff Sultan, quoted as saying there had been a clash in the Cleveland Advocate and no clash in the Tulsa Star. Sources disagreed on whether a motorcycle accident cited as a cause struck a Hungarian boy or an Italian girl, or killed an Italian boy.

reader.title: Chicago Heights race-riot scare
bases: The papers report threats, a gathering of Italians at a house where a Black family lived, a reported exodus of Black residents and the posting of deputies and guardsmen, but no confirmed attack, injury or property damage; the riot itself is denied by local officials and the Black press (A1, A3, A5, A20, A24).

Wire reports of rioting and a mass exodus (A1, A3) are contradicted by the police chief, the mayor, a Black resident and the Associated Negro Press (A5, A23, A24), though all agree that tension existed and deputies were sent (A1, A4, A21).

framing.detail: Universal Service headline 'Italians Drive Negroes in Droves From Chicago Heights Following Attempted Assault' put the alleged attack on a girl first.
AP follow-ups ran under heads such as 'Chicago Heights Riots Minimized' and 'No Rioting in Chicago Heights', quoting the chief.
Weekly digests in North Dakota and Nevada repeated the mobilization and alleged-attack story after the denials.
The Chicago Whip headlined 'Daily Paper Invents Story' and blamed the 'commercialized press' and white reporters for stirring race hatred.
The ANP item called the riot 'without foundation' and said news articles had magnified the strain.
